newsitem.title: USA: US CORPORATE BONDS - Supply on horizon, tobacco off.
newsitem.headline: US CORPORATE BONDS - Supply on horizon, tobacco off.

text.p: U.S. investment-grade and high-yield corporate bonds were waylayed on Monday as a full slate of issuer road shows and summer doldrums conspired to keep trading thin, dealers said.

Tobacco paper were again quoted softer, however, as repercussions from the Friday's proposed tobacco settlement sapped investor's confidences. But uncertainty over the deal capped activity and few trades were spotted on Monday.
One trader at a big New York shop likened commerce for tobacco bonds on Thursday to a Treasury trader setting positions before a potent economic indicator.

"The majority of the sellers came one to two days before the settlement came on Friday," the trader said. "I think now we just see a lot of people stand back and try to see where the bonds are going--they're not trading much in the Street."
Spreads of RJR Nabisco Holdings Inc issuers were quoted 15 to 20 basis points wider, while Philip Morris Cos bonds were about five basis points wider.
Elsewhere, investment grade spreads were largely unchanged with little stimulation from new issues or U.S. Treasuries lending the impetus to trade, dealers said.

The focus was fixated on forward supply, which includes a $2.75 billion taxable municipal bond deal from the New Jersey Economic Development Authority, a minimum of $600 million in debt from British Aerospace Plc, $500 million in 10-year debt from Sears Roebuck Acceptance Corp and up to $750 million in 144a trust preferreds from SAFECO Corp.

Turning to high-yields, at least 18 new issues set for pricing this week tabled trades for most of the session except for a late-day flurry, traders said. Prices were on the "softer side" but that was due more to summer apathy than reaction to the sharp sell-off in U.S. stocks, they said.

The Dow industrial average posted the second-largest single-day drop in its history, unofficially closing down 192 points or 2.5 percent. Comments from Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto about the potential sale of U.S. government securities prompted the wave of profit-taking, analysts said, and subsequent selling in Treasuries.
The benchmark 30-year bond closed down 17/32 to yield 6.70 percent. Bond prices had been higher for much of the session.

Despite the weaker performance of high-yields over the past several days, market participants said the week's multi-billion dollar supply calendar should garner adequate investor interest. More than 18 issues are scheduled.
"Deals haven't been trading up a point or two like they used to, but deals are still going to come tight," one trader said. "Performance of late might cost them 1/8 point but that's it."
Junk bond deals priced on Monday included:

--$200 million 9.75 percent B1/B-plus rated senior subordinated notes from Shoppers Food Warehouse Corp via Wasserstein Perella Securities (Grantchester) at par to yield 341 basis points over the Treasury curve.

--$175 million 8.875 percent 10-year B1/B-plus rated senior notes from DI Industries Inc via Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities at 99.508 to yield 8.95 percent or 256 basis points over the curve.
The DI Industries deal was increased in size by $50 million. It also priced tighter than 9 percent preliminary price talk, sources said.
